extracted.intended_audience: students, mathematicians, and general readers interested in the philosophy and practice of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of core practices and standards in mathematical thought: how to idealize and extract abstractions, generalize, formalize for machines, treat existence of objects, and the role of proof. Focus is on principles that guide producing and judging mathematical models, definitions, and texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction as idealization
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace concrete, physical instances by idealized mathematical objects (e.g., a physical pencil line vs. the ideal straight line; ideal straight line defined by properties or axioms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strip away accidentals and imperfections (weight, hardness, heat) and keep only quantity and spatial continuity; define objects by how they act or combine (axioms). Recognize that idealized mathematical deductions can only be approximately verified in the real world (e.g., angle bisectors in a drawn triangle are only approximately concurrent). Use idealization to make complex physical conditions tractable, but be explicit about the simplifying assumptions made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical modeling: state and justify assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming mathematical models of physical systems, explicitly state the simplifying assumptions needed to derive the model (example: deriving the one-dimensional wave equation for a vibrating string).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List assumptions such as perfect flexibility, constant linear density p, constant tension T, motion confined to a plane, small displacements/angles, no external forces, fixed boundary conditions, and initial conditions. Acknowledge that these assumptions are not exactly true but are approximately satisfied in many cases; declare boundary and initial conditions and check approximate validity before using model conclusions for real-world inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction as extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Form abstractions by extracting common features from diverse concrete instances (e.g., the number 'four' abstracted from groups of birds or oranges; graphs abstracted from geometric labyrinth plans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent only the information relevant to the problem (e.g., traversability of a maze), discard inessential geometric detail, and encode the remaining relations in combinatorial or set-theoretic data (incidence matrices, labeled nodes and edges). Use set-theoretic descriptions when useful (e.g., Russell and Whitehead viewpoint). Choose the simplest representation adequate for the task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of representation: keep only what matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the simplest visual or symbolic representation that preserves the properties of interest (e.g., replacing a complex floorplan by a simpler graph when only traversals matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not carry over unnecessary geometric or concrete detail that does not affect the phenomena under study; favor representations that facilitate conceptual and combinatorial reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization as broadening and consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Move from particular statements to more general ones by weakening hypotheses or changing the environment (e.g., equilateral -> isosceles triangle; 2D/3D diagonal formula -> n-dimensional generalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalization can strengthen results (fewer hypotheses), consolidate many related facts into a single economical statement, and expand the domain of applicability. Be aware that generalization may change conclusions (or make specific particular privileges unavailable) and may lose interesting particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions about generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: General facts do not necessarily capture all aspects of the particular; particulars may grant additional privileges lost in generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand what information and special properties are lost when passing to a general theory (e.g., equilateral-triangle theory is not contained entirely in isosceles-triangle theory), and decide whether consolidation or retention of particulars is more appropriate for the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization: adapting mathematics for mechanical processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate mathematical texts into a formal language (typically set theory) so they can be mechanically or algorithmically manipulated (e.g., axioms of Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem displayed in formal language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the motives for formalization (historically increased rigor; more recently machine processing and software). Understand that every mathematical text can, in principle, be formalized in a single formal language (set theory). Study and use the formal syntax and axioms (extensionality, empty set, union, infinity, replacement, power set, choice, regularity) when foundational precision or machine verification is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of axiom systems as foundational standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on explicit axiom systems (e.g., Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem axioms) to define and justify existence and operations in formalized mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide translations of formal axioms into natural language; be aware that acceptance of certain objects (e.g., ultrafilters) depends on acceptance of particular axioms (e.g., Axiom of Choice). Use axioms to define which constructions are legitimate in the chosen formal framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing mathematics for humans vs. machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate stylistic rules depending on the audience: formalized (machine) texts must leave nothing unstated; human-oriented texts should omit purely mechanical steps that distract from ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For machines: state every detail and mechanical step. For human readers: omit steps that are purely mechanical and instead present starting points, final results, and the constructive ideas that justify omitted steps. Supply the new idea that justifies non-mechanical steps; avoid overwhelming the reader with routine detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and construction of mathematical structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify a structure by its signature: a carrier set S, a set of operations or relations defined on S, and any distinguished elements (e.g., <R, +, ×, 0, 1> for real numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving definitions, state the signature and the axioms (laws of combination) that the signature must satisfy (e.g., semigroup: <S, ◦> with associative law; monoid: <S, ◦, 1> with identity). Use this approach to make clear what is meant by an 'object' vs. a 'structure' and to enable formal reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of mathematical objects is context-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical object's 'existence' depends on the setting, the demands placed upon it, and the axioms adopted (examples: √2 exists in reals; the 'moser' exists as a program/rule; the Fréchet ultrafilter exists in systems accepting the Axiom of Choice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge existence pragmatically by how one interacts with, constructs, or manipulates the object (writing it down, answering questions about it, or providing construction rules). Recognize multiple notions of existence (literary/diagrammatic vs. zoological vs. formal/mathematical) and state which notion is intended when asserting existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of large or highly abstract constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Large or highly abstract mathematical entities (huge integers, ultrafilters, hyperreals) are acceptable provided there are clear definitions, rules of construction, or demonstrations of utility within the adopted framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit constructive descriptions or formal definitions (programs, replacement rules, axiomatic acceptance) to make sense of enormous or non-intuitive objects. Anticipate psychological resistance and address existence via manipulability, definability, or dependence on accepted axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of proof in mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof is a central distinguishing feature of mathematics: it demonstrates truths especially when statements are not self-evident; some hold that 'no proof, no mathematics,' though this view is debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize proof's function in establishing certainty for non-transparent claims; in exposition aim to convey the constructive ideas behind proofs rather than every mechanical step; contextualize the role of proof philosophically when necessary.
